name: The Naming
description: You wake at the Hushline's edge with a Warden saying a name over you. Choose what you are called, put down what the mist coughs up, and ride to Merrowby.
notes: Stage numbers in quest_at and quest_stage are 1-based indices into stages. Stage 1 hands off to character creation (the Naming); the dialogue sets the flag 'named' when it is done.

stages.journal: Someone is saying a name, over and over, the way you would call a dog you were not sure was yours. Behind you is a grey mist with no colour in it. In front of you is a woman in a grey-green cloak who has plenty. She says she is a Warden. She wants to know what you are called, and she is not going to guess.

The mist has let out three of Greyfold's un-ended. They wave. Wren says to put them down and not to feel bad about it, and that the second part is harder than the first. Keep something in your legs; swing when they stumble.

There is a Hearthstone at Pilgrim's Ash, in the lee of a bell the size of a house that somebody lives in. Wren says: put your hand on the stone and say the name again, so the stone has it too. That is how you come back, if you go.

A carter is going north to Merrowby with a load of grey pilgrims' bells for melting. Wren has bought you a seat with the Wardens' marks and will want them back. She says the Vale is warmer than this, and then, after a moment, that this is not saying much.

name: The Toll Hums
description: Merrowby's bell is humming for the first time in living memory. Find out what the village thinks, go up inside the Toll, and take what you find to the Wardens.
notes: Stage numbers in quest_at and quest_stage are 1-based indices into stages.

stages.journal: Merrowby is built around a hole with a bell in it, and the bell is humming. It has not done that in living memory, which in Merrowby means since Pellam Ashcombe was a boy. Wren went ahead on a faster cart. Find her at the crater rim before the whole village finds you.

Wren wants to know what the village makes of the hum before the Wardens make anything of it. Start with the baker; everything in Merrowby starts with the baker. Then the innkeeper, whose cellar is the inside of the bell. Then old Pellam, who says he has heard it before, and who is the only person in the Vale nobody accuses of exaggerating.

Tobin has unbarred the cellar door that is not a cellar door. Past the casks the floor turns to bronze and slopes upward inside the bell: the Toll's lip. Something up in the crown is doing the humming. Pellam says the Builders wrote on the inside of everything they made, and that nobody has climbed high enough to read it since his father.

In the crown of the Toll there was a cradle of black stone with a tine in it, and the tine was humming a half-note below the bell, as if they had fallen out. Wren has taken it to Wardens' Rest. The Roll room is where the names of vanished villages are kept; she says if the hum means anything, it will be written there before it is written anywhere else.

There is a fourth line on the Roll since Tollday. Harewell: a hamlet on the down between Merrowby and Tamwick, eleven households, a well with a hare cut on its lip. You do not know it. Nobody does. That is the point. Wren says the Sayers in Tollmere will pronounce on the tine and the hum together, and that they will charge for it. She is writing you a letter, because a letter is cheaper than a Warden.

name: Louder Than Books
description: Take the tine and Wren's letter to the Sayers' Circle in Tollmere. Hear three lectures that cannot all be right, and learn the Circle's price.
notes: Stage numbers in quest_at and quest_stage are 1-based indices into stages.

stages.journal: Wren's letter is addressed to 'whichever of the Circle is speaking this week'. Tollmere is across the Long Stride causeway, on an island of black stone the Builders left and the guilds built on top of. She says to keep one hand on your purse and the other on your name.

The Sayers' Spire is a black Oroth stalk with a brass crown that people built later, like a hat on a standing stone. The Sayer at the door, Aldith Sulion, reads Wren's letter twice and says the Circle will hear you, which she pronounces as if it were a fee.

Three Sayers, three lectures, three answers to the hum. Sulion says a note is shifting and the Toll can hear it. Cresswell says the village is talking about it, which in his account is the same thing as it being true. Ondrael says something is breathing in. They cannot all be right. They are all certain. Ask each what the others get wrong; that is where the Circle keeps its honesty.

The Circle will pronounce on the tine and on the hum, together, in council, for a price: the bell from the altar of the Drowned Nave, west across the marsh, which the Sayers have wanted for three hundred years and which the reedfolk have never offered. Bennick Cresswell caught you on the stair and said, quietly, that the reedfolk would tell you what the water kept for nothing at all, if you were willing to wait for it.

options.text: Take the Circle's errand. Fetch the Nave Bell for the Sayers.
Decline the price. Go west to the reedfolk on your own account.

name: What the Water Kept
description: Wait on the boards of Isseva, go down into the Drowned Nave for the bell, and learn from the reedfolk what the tide does not take.
notes: Stage numbers in quest_at and quest_stage are 1-based indices into stages.

stages.journal: Isseva stands on stilts in a fog that smells of peat and eel-oil, and every third pole has a lantern on it. The Reed Council's eldest is Tallissa Oul. The reedfolk are warm to anyone who waits, so: wait.

Tallissa Oul will not answer a question until you have sat down, and will not answer this one until you have slept a night on the boards and heard what the marsh sounds like when the lanterns go out. Isseva's Hearthstone is on the burial jetty, among the hooks the dead go out on.

The Drowned Nave leans out of the marsh like the mast of something too big to have sunk. Its lower half is water, and the water rises when someone sings in it. She Who Waits is on the altar and has been for longer than Isseva has had a name, and the bell the Circle wants is in her lap. Tallissa said: she is not your enemy, only in your way, and that this is true of most things in the marsh. Break her hymn when she starts it, or it will mend her.

The bell rings when nobody speaks. The Circle wants it on a shelf in Tollmere; Tallissa wants it back in the water with a lantern, because it is the Nave's and the Nave is the marsh's now. You could also simply keep it, which nobody has suggested and everybody has thought of.

options.text: The Circle asked first. The bell goes to Tollmere.
It belongs to the water. Give it to Tallissa for the jetty.
Keep it. A bell that rings for silence might be useful to someone who came out of the Hush.

stages.journal: Tallissa will tell you the Tide now, and the thing the reedfolk know that the Sayers do not: the water takes everything back in its time, except one thing. There is a note in the south that the tide does not reach. She says the Builders' Seat is holding something, the way a hand holds a fish that would rather be in the river, and that a held thing does not rot, and does not rest either.

name: A Hand on the Rope
description: Be held by the mountain, hear the Rope-Song, and take a name back from the Stone-Thrall King in the singing shaft.
notes: Stage numbers in quest_at and quest_stage are 1-based indices into stages.

stages.journal: The clans measure a stranger by the deeds they have heard of. Kharrow Hold is carved into a cliff above a gorge and reached by a bridge of chain that sings in the wind. The memory-keeper is Dunna ko-Kharrow. If she has not heard of you, she will say so, and the conversation will be short.

Dunna ko-Kharrow will sing the Rope-Song for you, but the clans do not sing to people the mountain has not held. Go up to the Fallen Hand, lie a night in the palm where the shrine is, and come back with the cold still in you. She will know if you cheated; she says the Hand leaves a mark on the back that takes a week to fade.

The Rope-Song has a verse for each of the seven clans and a hole where an eighth should be. Dunna says the eighth clan went down into the Choir when the Choir was new, to sing with the Builders, and was breathed in. The Stone-Thrall King in the singing shaft of Oskeld is what is left of them: their weight without their name. Whoever gets the name out of him gives it back to the Moot, or does not.

The Oskeld shaft sings when the wind is right, and the King walks in it. Break what you can of him and he will fight differently with what is left; the clans say he is not a person and about half of them believe it. When the shaft's echo starts to stagger you, ride the cart chain up to his head.

The name was in the King the way a tune is in a bell: Ghorr, the Bone Clan, who went down to sing and were breathed in. Say it to Dunna and it goes into the Rope-Song and into every child in the Hold by winter. Keep it, and the mountain is a little lighter and a little emptier, and the shaft will not sing again. Dunna has an opinion. She will honour yours.

options.text: Give the Moot its eighth verse. Say the name: Ghorr.
Let the Bone Clan go. Some names are a weight, not a rope.

name: The Briar's Purpose
description: Walk the failing Briar with the Woodfolk, stand in the Standing Moot against its keeper, and learn what the wall was grown to keep in.
notes: Stage numbers in quest_at and quest_stage are 1-based indices into stages.

stages.journal: The Woodfolk have no law, only custom and bows. Alder Wyke at Fernhold walks the Briar every morning and counts the grey patches in it. He will not tell a stranger what the count is, but he will show you, which among Woodfolk is the more generous thing.

The Thornmarch is a wall of living thorn, vines as thick as arms, grown on purpose by people who wrote no purpose down. There are grey patches in it now where the thorn has gone brittle and colourless, and beyond the grey patches the air is very still and the birds do not go.

Custom says the Standing Moot answers one question of whoever stands at its centre at dusk and is still standing at dark. The Hart of Thorns has kept the circle since before the Woodfolk had a word for keeping, and he has never let anyone stand that long. Alder says the Hart is not a villain, only a keeper who has forgotten what he is keeping the circle from, and that this is a thing that happens to keepers.

The stones hum when you stand in the middle. The Hart charges when you stand in the middle. Use the stones to break his charge, and mind the Briar when it starts to grow across the circle; it grows fast, and it bleeds you, and the arena will be half the size before you notice.

The circle answered at dark, the way Alder said it would, in a voice that was mostly the hum: the Briar was grown by the Builders to keep the Hush in the south when the Seat's note went wrong; it is failing because the note is failing; and the Seat opens only for the ones who have kept vigil over it. Custom says whoever felled the keeper keeps the Moot. You may keep it, name a Woodfolk keeper, or leave the centre empty and let the circle decide what that means.

options.text: Keep the Moot yourself. Its answer was given to you.
Name Alder Wyke keeper. It is the Woodfolk's circle.
Leave the centre empty. Nobody should keep a thing that long.

name: The Held Note
description: Keep one night's vigil with the Tolling Order, open the Cantor's Seat with your name, face the one who has held the note for a thousand years, and decide what note the world holds next.
notes: Stage numbers in quest_at and quest_stage are 1-based indices into stages. The third ending option needs renown 600 and the flag ranked_in_a_faction, which every faction line's first quest sets on completion; the Wardens' line (systems stream) should set it too.

stages.journal: The Tolling Order has kept vigil over the Choir for a hundred and seventy-seven years, waiting for someone the Seat would open for. Cadwen Ash says the door opens for the known, and asks, without unkindness, how known you are.

One night's vigil at the Choir, by the Order's custom, before the Seat. Twelve headless colossi in a ring; one bell every few minutes from somewhere; the note underneath everything. Cadwen will walk the ring with you and count the bells. Sleep first; she says nobody should meet the Cantor tired, and that he will not mind waiting, having done so much of it.

The door of the Seat has no hinges and opens for names. Cadwen said yours, and the Order's, and the names of the knights who did not come back, and the door opened on the third of those, which she did not comment on. Inside, the note-light is a cold blue that has burned for a thousand years, and there is someone sitting in it.

The Cantor is holding the note the way you would hold a door shut against a wind: with the whole body, for a thousand years, with no idea any longer of what is on the other side. First the bell-blade. Then the Choir on the balconies, who can be silenced or endured. Then the note itself, when colour goes out of the room and only what you have been named for stays lit. Stand where you are known.

The note is in your hands now, and it is heavier than the Cantor made it look. Let it end, and the deep places go quiet and empty, the dead rest, and the Dwindling comes on faster and honestly. Hold it, and the world keeps as it is, and your name is the price: nobody will say it again, and you will sit here. Or, if you are known enough, sing a new one: strike the Toll again with everything that has been said about you. The Toll will not survive it. Merrowby will have to learn to live without a bell.

options.text: Hold the note. Take the Seat.
Sing a new note. Strike the Toll with your name.
